rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The retention pattern will guide a narrower gradient window and targeted slope or temperature changes.
Injection 1 already achieves the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether the run can be faster while keeping every pair fully resolved.

Test the next shorter gradient to establish the speed limit at 40 C and measure the critical pair’s slope sensitivity. Injection 2 remains a fully resolved, maximum-score fallback if that pair drops below R = 1.5.

Test whether higher temperature changes selectivity enough to resolve the critical pair at the six-minute gradient while further shortening retention. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect.

Use a slightly shallower six-minute gradient to recover critical-pair resolution, with an intermediate temperature to avoid the early-pair co-elution seen at 60 C. The endpoint remains well above the observed elution window.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to lift the critical pair above R = 1.5 while preserving the favorable selectivity at 50 C. This should recover the maximum score with an earlier last peak than injection 2.

Shift the gradient window upward while retaining injection 6’s slope and temperature to remove time spent at low organic fraction. Test whether this shortens retention without sacrificing full resolution, particularly for the early and critical middle pairs.

Slightly flatten injection 7’s gradient to restore the middle pair’s resolution while retaining the time savings from the higher starting organic fraction. The other pairs have ample resolution margin.

Trim the gradient window and raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention, while using a slightly shallower slope to protect the critical middle pair. The endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction of 0.51.
Increase the endpoint by one grid step to shorten the run using injection 9’s resolution margin. This tests whether the critical middle pair remains above R = 1.5 at a slightly steeper gradient.

Raise the starting organic fraction to reduce retention while keeping the endpoint at 0.60, making the gradient shallower to protect the critical middle pair. Monitor the early pair closely because its resolution may decrease at the higher starting fraction.

With a maximum-score method secured, test a much steeper gradient at lower temperature for a faster, alternative selectivity regime. The critical middle pair may separate again after an elution-order reversal, while lower temperature should help retain the early compounds.

Explore the fast-gradient regime with a higher starting fraction to shift middle-pair selectivity and shorten retention. A moderate temperature increase may improve the late pair’s separation without the early-pair compression observed at 60 C.

Test whether a higher starting fraction and lower temperature strengthen separation of the critical middle pair in the fast-gradient regime. Lower temperature also helps preserve retention and separation of the early peaks.

Test a higher starting fraction to change middle-pair selectivity while the narrower gradient span may improve late-pair resolution. This is exploratory: the first peak may become nearly unretained, so early-pair separation must also be checked.

Reduce the endpoint by one-tenth to test the critical middle pair’s slope response in this fast, high-starting-organic regime. The early pair remains resolved, and the late pair should have more room under the shallower gradient.

Test a substantially narrower gradient window to improve the middle pair, whose resolution increased only slightly in injection 16. The stronger final hold may extend late retention, but this method could still be faster than the fully resolved benchmark.

The critical pair responded weakly to gradient slope at 25 C, so test temperature-driven selectivity with injection 16’s gradient unchanged. Check early-pair resolution carefully because higher temperature will further reduce its retention.

Test whether a higher starting fraction improves middle-pair selectivity enough for full resolution with a short gradient. Keep temperature low to protect the early pair, whose resolution is likely to become the limiting constraint.

Return to the fastest fully resolved method and isolate a five-degree temperature decrease. This will show whether lower temperature improves its narrow resolution margins before further gradient acceleration.

Use the six-minute grid to obtain a slope between injections 9 and 10, targeting full resolution near their faster retention limit. Returning to 50 C favors the critical middle pair while preserving early-pair separation.

Test a modest slope increase over injection 11 using the finer slope increment available with a six-minute gradient. This targets a shorter fully resolved run, though the middle pair’s small resolution margin makes this a boundary test.

Test whether a five-degree temperature increase lifts injection 10’s critical middle pair above R = 1.5 while shortening retention. The early pair may lose resolution, so this checks the temperature boundary rather than assuming an improvement.

Back off one endpoint step from injection 22 to restore middle-pair resolution while retaining adequate early-pair separation. This tests a slightly shallower, potentially more robust alternative to injection 11, which remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Use the final injection to test a more robust maximum-score alternative: a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 should improve middle-pair resolution while preserving early-pair separation. Injection 11 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method; the maximum CRF is already secured.
